title: Buy One Get One
description:
{name} is stringing together short-term jobs to cover his living expenses. Unable to sleep before dawn, he steps into a lit 24-hour convenience store.

He sets a triangle gimbap on the counter and reaches for his card. The clerk points to a small red sign on the shelf.

"That one's two-for-one today. You can grab another one."

{name} misses the sign. She could simply scan the one he brought, but she points out the offer first.
A stranger's face across the register. He does not know her name yet.

choices.text: Thank her, then ask her name
choices.result_text:
"...I didn't realize. Thank you."
The clerk smiles. "I'm Kim Daeun. I work the night shift."

{name} gives his name too. For the first time, they call each other by name.

choices.text: Thank her and leave
choices.result_text:
{name} gives a small bow and steps outside.
It is not a night when he has room to draw a stranger into a longer conversation.

The bag holds two triangle gimbap for the price he expected to pay for one. He does not ask the clerk's name.

title: 6:10 A.M.
description:
At 1:13 on Saturday morning, {name} sent the first message.

"Daeun, want to get breakfast after your shift this week? I'll wait for you."

Her answer was as short as a barcode. "6:10. Thirty minutes, that's all. If you're late, I'm leaving."

At 6:06, {name} was already seated in a twenty-four-hour gimbap shop two blocks from the convenience store. Daeun came in wearing a gray hoodie, slipping her night-shift name tag into its pocket. Without a register between them, she seemed unsure where to put her hands.

"You really did get here first."
"I was the one who made the appointment."

As the menu lay between them, a new work schedule lit up {name}'s phone. It asked for an answer by 6:30. Daeun saw the light and checked the wall clock. Their thirty minutes rested on the table as if they had not begun yet.

choices.text: Settle the work schedule first, then spend whatever time remains together
choices.result_text:
{name} traded messages about start times and shift conditions. By the time the confirmation arrived, the wall clock read 6:24.

Daeun unfolded the menu she had put away. "You weren't late, exactly. But this is pretty close to not showing up, {name}."

{name} had secured the shift and lost the time it took to order. For the few minutes left, they shared two cartons of convenience-store milk instead of a hot bowl of soup.

choices.text: Say it first: "I asked because I wanted to see you"
choices.result_text:
Daeun's hand stopped over her water glass. "You're supposed to say things like that after we order, {name}. It's less startling."

It was not a refusal. She hid reddening ears behind the strings of her hood and pointed to two rolls of gimbap and one bowl of udon. At 6:30, the face-down phone buzzed once and the work standby list closed. An empty plate settled between them.

choices.text: Let Daeun choose the food and what they talk about first
choices.result_text:
"Udon first, then. It tastes awful cold. We can talk after."

Daeun chose what she wanted, not simply the cheapest thing on the menu. After the order slip went to the kitchen, the 6:30 alert appeared and the unanswered work slot went to someone else. {name} turned the phone facedown. Everything they had not asked stayed there until the steam rose.

title: Forty Minutes Outside the Store
description:
At four on Sunday afternoon, Daeun was just ending her shift when {name} opened the convenience-store door. Another clerk took the register. Daeun pulled on a faded navy cardigan and placed tofu and eggs with discount stickers in her grocery bag. Today she was no longer the clerk, and {name} had not yet chosen anything to buy.

"It feels strange seeing you away from the counter, {name}."

Beside the red chairs outside, Daeun checked the arrival time for her bus. A notice for this month's housing payment remained on {name}'s phone. Beyond the store sign, a path followed the stream. If he said nothing now, Daeun would carry her bag to the stop. {name} had to decide how to ask for her time.

description_memory_if_known.relationship_memory:daeun:daeun_tuesday_: Before dawn last Tuesday, {name} had actually come at the time he named. That was why Daeun did not dismiss today's question as a courtesy. She looked up from the bus schedule.

choices.text: Ask her to have dinner nearby now that her shift is over — spend more of today with her
choices.result_text:
When {name} said, "Dinner is on me," Daeun hesitated as if she too had seen the housing-payment notice. Then she set the boundary first. "Nowhere expensive."

They sat by the steamed-up window of a small bunsik shop. Daeun talked about the nights when sleep still would not come after her shift. {name} did not add an answer; he listened to the end. The bill stayed pinned under a water glass. One bus had already passed.

choices.text: Ask her to walk for forty minutes, then keep the next obligation
choices.result_text:
Daeun closed the bus screen. "Forty minutes works. I already finished my shopping." {name} set an alarm and pointed toward the stream.

When it sounded, he stopped without making an excuse. "I have to end it here today."

Instead of saying she was disappointed, Daeun adjusted the handles of her grocery bag. "Precise, aren't you? Still better than disappearing without a word." They parted at the corner where the convenience-store light returned.

choices.text: Open the notebook and ask whether he may explain why he wrote down 3 billion won and Gangnam
choices.result_text:
{name} opened his worn notebook. Three billion won. Five years. Gangnam. Daeun studied the grooves pressed into the paper longer than the numbers themselves.

"I don't think this is a story we can finish before my bus arrives. Come to the store tonight. Tell me then why it has to be Gangnam."

That night, {name} waited outside the convenience-store doors with the notebook in his pocket until the customers thinned. His prepared answer and the true one split apart on opposite sides of the glass.

title: The Dream
description:
When the late-night convenience store emptied, only the refrigerator motor remained. Folding the lid of his ramyeon cup, {name} said, "Within five years, I'll be living in Gangnam with 3 billion won in assets."

Daeun's hand stopped over the barcode scanner. She gave a short laugh of surprise, then grew serious. "That's a very big dream. But why Gangnam, {name}?"

{name} looked down at the steam rising from the cup. He had prepared an answer about success and status. Daeun's eyes held no contempt, only a quiet curiosity waiting for whatever he had hidden behind that answer.

choices.text: "Because I never want to be looked down on again." — give her the hidden reason
choices.result_text:
For the first time, {name} spoke about shrinking before anyone could discover he was poor, and avoiding people's eyes through the years spent paying his father's debt. The steam blurred his sight as the words continued.

Daeun rested both hands on the counter and listened to the end. "I understand. But where you live doesn't give anyone permission to look down on you, {name}."

No one had ever taken his side before taking the side of his goal. Her sentence remained above the cooling broth.

choices.text: "It's just the symbol of success." — use the answer he prepared
choices.result_text:
{name} smiled and used the answer he had prepared. Daeun watched for another moment, then said, "I see," and returned to arranging the register. The scanner's red line passed between them.

Their conversation moved on to rent and the night shift. It stayed light and safe, catching on nothing.

As he carried the ramyeon toward the door, {name} felt as if one unasked question remained behind the counter.

title: Fork in the Road
description:
At the convenience store before dawn, Daeun got a call from home. Her mother was unwell, and a stable position had opened at the local market in her hometown.

"...I think I may pack up here and go back. Seoul is just too much."

She looked at {name}. She did not ask him to become her reason to stay, or to let her go. Only the unasked question remained in her eyes.

{name} thought Daeun would be the only name he had to answer that week. For now.

choices.text: "Don't go. Let's hold on here together" — reach for her
choices.result_text:
She was quiet for a moment, then smiled softly.
"...Okay. I'll stay a little longer. But don't leave 'we'll endure it together' as something you only said tonight."

Daeun reached beneath the counter and brought out two sheets she had folded and unfolded all night.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let her go
choices.result_text:
{name} could not open his mouth. He told himself he could not afford to be anchored now.

Daeun smiled faintly, said "Take care," then turned and removed her store badge. Just as the goal felt sharp again, the sound of her unfolding the bus sheet kept that conclusion from closing.

title: The Cost of 'Together'
description:
One sheet listed a month of Seoul rent, transit, and night shifts. The other showed the first bus home and the terms of the mart job.

Daeun pushed the Seoul sheet toward {name}. "Write down a promise that will still be alive next week, when you're busy. If the plan makes me pay the whole cost of staying, that isn't us enduring it together."

The first commuter bus passed beyond the automatic doors. The words asking her to stay were over. Now he had to write the time and cost those words would occupy.

choices.text: Place his housing notice beside hers and write Saturday at two and the costs he will carry
choices.result_text:
{name} placed his housing notice beside Daeun's table. He circled Saturday at two, then divided the rent and travel time into the parts he would carry.

"Don't just write half. Write the days you can't come too."

Daeun slid him the calculator. They wrote the dates most likely to fail before the easy promises. One sentence about enduring together became a full page of responsibility.

choices.text: Book two seats on the first bus home and ask to hear her answer again there
choices.result_text:
Instead of touching the Seoul budget, {name} opened the bus app. "I shouldn't decide Seoul for you just because I asked you to stay. This weekend I'll go with you and see your mother and the mart. I'll hear your answer again there."

Daeun did not thank him right away. After a long pause, she wrote both names beside the first Saturday bus. Neither the Seoul sheet nor the hometown sheet was thrown away. Only the hours of that weekend were settled.

title: The Sentence of the One Who Lets Go
description:
Daeun opened two sheets beside the badge she had removed. Seoul rent and night shifts filled one set of columns; daytime work and hours near her mother filled the other.

"Don't say you're letting me go for my sake. I lose something if I leave too." Daeun turned the pen toward {name}. "Tell me what you preserve by not asking me to stay. Then this won't be only my choice."

The first bus appeared on the arrival board beyond the glass. Even silence now needed the name of the person who chose it.

choices.text: Say, "Right now, I'm choosing Seoul and the goal over us"
choices.result_text:
{name} did not avoid her eyes. "Right now, I'm choosing Seoul and the goal over us. I won't pretend you're leaving because home is easier."

Daeun did not thank him. She crossed his name out of one line on the Seoul budget and folded the sheet for home. Without an excuse, the sentence that remained belonged to both of them.

choices.text: Do not call it Daeun's choice; write that he did not ask her to stay
choices.result_text:
On the back of the Seoul sheet, {name} wrote one line. Not 'Daeun is leaving,' but 'I did not ask her to stay.'

Daeun read it and capped the pen. "That's enough."

Cold dawn air entered when the automatic doors opened. Daeun promised no next meeting, and {name} did not add another take-care.

title: Two Addresses
description:
The convenience-store badge Daeun had removed smelled faintly of coffee and plastic from the night. At 6:42 a.m., she placed it beneath the counter and laid two sheets beside it, creased from a night of folding. One listed a month of Seoul rent, transit, and night shifts. The other showed the first bus home and the terms for a steady job at the hometown mart.

"Mom is ill, and a stable position opened at the mart. If I go back, I can work days and stay near her. I can't tell whether Seoul is still my dream or I'm only afraid to go home."

Daeun pushed both sheets toward {name} without asking him to make her stay. "Don't ask which place is easier, Minjun. Neither one is. Look at what Seoul costs and what I would leave behind at home."

The first commuter bus passed beyond the automatic doors. Neither address was crossed out.

choices.text: Divide the cost of staying in Seoul between them
choices.result_text:
{name} took out his housing notice and placed it beside Daeun's Seoul budget. Under the figures he drew two columns: "Daeun alone" and "what we can carry together."

Daeun slid the calculator toward him. "Don't just write half. This plan has to survive the days you're too busy to be here."

They added travel time and days off beside the rent. The promise to endure together took one sentence; the table required the entire page.

choices.text: Go with Daeun to her hometown first this weekend
choices.result_text:
{name} opened the bus app and selected the first departure.

"If you come with me, won't we have to decide there?"

"No. First I'll look and listen. We decide after that."

After a long pause, Daeun circled Saturday. She did not fold the Seoul budget or throw away the page for home. Only the open hours of that weekend were closed first, under both their names.

choices.text: Do not ask her to wait; listen to the choice she makes
choices.result_text:
{name} turned both sheets back toward her. "I won't ask you to stay because of me. I'll listen to the answer you choose."

Daeun did not thank him. "Don't say it like you're sending me somewhere easier. I lose something if I go home too. This weekend I'll go down alone and see Mom and the mart job first. I'll decide about the room in Seoul after that."

When {name} nodded, she folded both pages. They stood at the automatic doors without writing another appointment. The first bus stopped outside, and Daeun gestured for him to board before her.

title: First Time Out
description:
She asked: "Want to go somewhere with me today?"

First time. Daeun outside the convenience store.

They ended up at a nearby tent bar — pojangmacha.
One bottle of soju. One serving of kimchi pancake.

She was different away from the counter.
A little more relaxed. A little more laughing.

He said "they should sell triangular kimbap here" and she burst out laughing.
A real laugh.

choices.text: "Today is enough." — Gangnam forgotten for a moment
choices.result_text: Gangnam slipped out of his head for a moment. Strangely, that felt good.

choices.text: "Next time I'll take you somewhere better" — today feels like too little
choices.result_text: Today was today. Whether it was enough — not really sure.

title: The Reason at 3 A.M.
description:
3 A.M.

A message from Daeun.
"You awake? ...Just can't sleep. Not exactly struggling — just."

{name} stared at the screen, then looked out the window. Seoul doesn't go dark at 3 A.M.

Three billion won was still far off. Time was always running short.

But right now, looking at this message — for the first time, it felt clear.
Why he was running.

choices.text: Reply: "Me too. Don't worry"
choices.result_text:
A short text exchange. Nothing important. Around 4 A.M. she fell asleep first.
{name} opened the laptop again. Wanted to win — for this person too.

choices.text: Send "Sleep well" — then open the laptop
choices.result_text: Can't afford to waver. But — why he's running felt a little clearer.

title: You and Gangnam
description:
Late. The sound of {name} clicking at a calculator woke Daeun.

She watched for a long time, then spoke quietly.
"...I get anxious sometimes."

{name} looked up, and she kept going.
"When you get to Gangnam... what happens to me?
You're the reason I stayed here,
but I don't know if the person who gets there will still want me."

The words hung in the air a long time.

{name} didn't know what to say.
There were things that couldn't be said yet — not until the right moment.

choices.text: "Even there, I won't forget the person who's here. Let's hold on together." — that was all
choices.result_text:
She nodded without a word.
The words fell short — but they got through.
The things he still couldn't put into words — maybe he'd say them someday, in Gangnam.

choices.text: "When I get to Gangnam I'll treat you better. Bear with it for now."
choices.result_text: She smiled — but that smile was a little sad. {name} knew it too.

choices.text: "Honestly I don't know. I need to think about that too."
choices.result_text: Couldn't answer. That silence stayed with him a long time.

choices.text: "Forget Gangnam — I need you here, now. Let's be together."
choices.result_text:
Daeun's eyes widened. The numbers on the calculator stayed still, but their light trembled faintly between them.

"...Do you mean it?"
"I do. Gangnam will still be there in five years. But you — you're here now."

Daeun did not smile right away. She looked at {name}'s hand resting on the calculator and pressed her lips together. Only after touching the reddened corner of one eye with the back of her hand did she nod.

"Then you don't get to say you weren't sure later."
"I won't."

She smiled. Neither of them hurried to fill the silence before it was finished.

That night, the distance that had lingered since the convenience-store counter disappeared. It was the first day they chose to walk the remaining four years together.

title: The Text That Never Sent
description:
Late at night, picked up the phone — and found himself in Daeun's contact.

Last message: 'Take care.' She'd sent it.
Below that — nothing.

He started typing.
'Hey, how have you been? You doing okay?'

Finger hovering over send.
Thinking about the ripple that one message would make in her life.

Deleted it.
Typed it again.
Deleted it again.

choices.text: Send it — a simple check-in is okay
choices.result_text:
A reply came back a little while later.
'Oh, hey. Doing fine :)'
That one emoji said a lot.
{name} set the phone down and looked out the window.

choices.text: Don't send it — going back into her life isn't right
choices.result_text:
Deleted.
The screen went black.
{name} stared at that dark screen for a long time.
I hope she's doing well. Truly. That's enough.
The most {name} could do, right now.

title: A Glimpse of Her
description:
Stumbled across it on social media.

A photo Daeun took back in her hometown.
In front of the mart. Side by side with her mom. One small potted plant. A bright smile.

'Doing just fine :)'

{name} looked at that photo for a long time.
She's okay. That thought arrived — and for some reason made the hollow feeling worse.
It only now fully landed that she was someone nowhere in Seoul anymore.

choices.text: Hit like — hope you're doing well. I'll do the same
choices.result_text:
He tapped like.
A moment later, a notification: 'Daeun liked your post.'

No short comment. {name} said nothing either.
That was enough. That was the end.

choices.text: Scroll past — pretend you didn't see it
choices.result_text:
{name} scrolled down.
The next post was a crypto ad.
Life continued.

Only the things that never quite arrived stayed behind.

title: A Rented Room in Winter
description:
Daeun dropped by often. Always with something in her hands.
A few eggs. Spinach. Tofu.

{name} would be staring at an investment screen and she'd reach over and touch the frame of his glasses.
"Your eyes are going to give out." That had become something they just said.

They weren't a couple. But just friends didn't quite cover it either — there was something more.
Neither of them put that line into words.

Somewhere along the way, her being here stopped feeling strange.
Whether that was good, or just habit — he wasn't sure.

choices.text: Decide to just cook something together tonight
choices.result_text: They dug through the fridge together. Nothing decent to work with — but that kind of evening wasn't bad.

choices.text: "I still can't give you much yet — is that okay?"
choices.result_text:
Daeun paused for a moment. "I'm not asking for that."
The words were plain. Something still unnamed sat quietly between them.

description_if_known.daeun_romance_started:
Daeun practically lives here now. She brings something every time.
A few eggs, spinach, tofu. One shelf of the fridge became hers without either of them deciding it.

When {name} stares at the trading screen, she reaches from behind and taps his glasses.
"You'll ruin your eyes." He's used to it now.

A few months since they became a couple. The tiny room never felt tiny.
At some point her being here became a given — and {name} learned, for the first time, that a given could feel this good.

title: The End of Waiting
description:
A message from Daeun.
"Can we talk for a bit?"

A side table at a pojangmacha. Two shots of soju.

"I've been thinking about it for a long time. It's not that you're a bad person —
but I have my own life too. I don't want waiting to become my life."

{name} had things to say. Things he should have said.
It felt too late for them now.

choices.text: "I'm sorry. You're right." Accept it.
choices.result_text:
She stood up. "I hope things work out for you. I mean that."
It sounded like the truth. That made it worse.

{name} sat there for a long time after she left.
The words 'just wait a little longer' — this was where they led.

choices.text: "Even now — I can change." Try to hold on.
choices.result_text:
She looked at {name} for a moment.
"It's not about you changing. I chose to wait too. I'm just tired of it."

That was the more honest answer.
{name} couldn't find a word to say.

title: The In-Between Distance
description:
They'd been seeing each other less.
No clear starting point for when.
No plans made. No avoidance either.
Just — both getting busy.

Today he ran into her on the street.
"Oh, hey." A long silence after that.
This had become their default.

They never officially ended things, so things never ended.
They never tried to continue, so things never continued.

choices.text: "Where does this leave us?" Ask her directly.
choices.result_text:
She thought for a while. Then: "...I don't know. Me neither."

Both of them not knowing — that was itself a kind of answer.
After that day, neither reached out. That was the answer too.

choices.text: "You doing okay?" Let it pass.
choices.result_text:
"Yeah, doing fine."
And they each went their separate way.

He didn't look back. More accurately — he didn't have the nerve to.
The silence from that night of 'I'm not sure' —
it ended like this.
